what: The sections of this article, each with a line and a paragraph, for showing what the reader has already read. Built by admin/build/summaries.py from admin/content/articles/summaries/.

sections.label: The opening
sections.line: Liquid content needs reporting kept as a graph
sections.para: FT Strategies' primer on liquid content is clear and mostly right. I would push on where the water comes from: the reporting itself, kept with sources as a graph. Put experienced journalists at the centre with better tools and affordable experts, keep writing theirs, and pay per use back to whoever found the facts.

sections.label: Liquid needs water
sections.line: The water is the reporting, not the format
sections.para: What must become liquid is the notebook, calls, documents, hypotheses and doubts, much of which never reaches the article. Clay loses its ingredients. A graph keeps claims with confidence, evidence with provenance, protected sources and contradictions as edges, so every projection, from article to agent answer, can say why it is true.

sections.label: The method already exists
sections.line: Journalism's method exists; the tools are the gap
sections.para: The guide calls for reinventing newsroom norms, which I think is a trap. Centuries of practice already supply the method; the inefficiency is in tools, since most reporting value is discarded at publication. Capture notes and calls as journalists already make them, and give each one a custom desk, now cheap to build.

sections.label: Writing is how the story is found
sections.line: Writing stays the journalist's, because it finds the story
sections.para: AI should not write everything from fed facts. Writing reveals the narrative and the holes, sending the reporter back out. The journalist's article is one projection of the graph and theirs; others, such as audio or translations, are checked against it. Discoveries and readers' unanswerable questions feed back into the graph.

sections.label: The experts a newsroom could rarely afford
sections.line: A graph makes paid, credited experts affordable per story
sections.para: Newsrooms rarely afforded a historian, data scientist, lawyer or industry insider for one story. A graph recording who supported which claim makes it economic to bring them in for an hour and pay them for time and credibility, which accumulates. Journalists should hear: we will make what you do better.

sections.label: The three "is not"s, with a graph underneath
sections.line: The three exclusions each change with a graph beneath
sections.para: Finished articles, including the FT's deep archive, can be liquefied, starting from one topic. Interfaces are fine if every answer names its claim and source. Personalisation should be the intersection of the reader's graph (role, sector, time, language) with the story's, as in the bridge simulation.

sections.label: Readers' tastes are not the brief
sections.line: Optimising for readers' tastes is the clickbait brief
sections.para: Read literally, prioritising readers' tastes is what gave us twenty years of clickbait. Readers pay for a publication's judgment: what matters, how it is checked and presented. A graph showing where claims come from makes points of view visible. Readers' needs should shape projections, not replace the editorial direction.

sections.label: How it pays
sections.line: A sourced graph adds payment per use beyond attention
sections.para: The guide's retention, dynamic advertising and licensing are still the attention economy; by 2017 Google and Meta took 54.7% of American digital advertising. A graph enables per-use reader payments, agents paying per question, evidence licensing and shares returning to journalists and contributors. Structure for AI engines has value its readers should pay for.

sections.label: Where I would start
sections.line: Start with one journalist, one topic, one graph
sections.para: Pick a topic and the reporter who knows it best. Capture their notebook as a graph they can correct, build them a desk, bring in one paid expert, publish their article plus one other projection, and measure. Then liquefy what the next story touches. Quotes are from Sofia Giannuzzi's FT Strategies guide.
